title: Noise structuring in fixed-depth Trotter simulation: stationary channels and observable-level depolarization
authors: G. L. Stavisskii, W. V. Pogosov, L. E. Fedichkin, A. V. Lebedev
abstract: We analyze fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body dynamics. The number of layers is chosen using the largest endpoint time and is then kept fixed throughout the time scan, making the total noise dose approximately independent of the endpoint time. For local stochastic faults, we show that, once propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, the noisy circuit factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary finite-depth binomial channel. In the dilute-layer limit, this channel reduces to a Poissonian exponential. The memory time of a single fault is related to a Loschmidt echo. An important consequence is observable-level depolarization: for selected macroscopic observables at low to moderate noise levels, the stationary channel can act as an almost time-independent affine contrast correction, even though the full channel need not be depolarizing, which is crusial for error mitigation purposes. At short times, the same protocol produces a digital Zeno-like transient, in which a fixed number of noise opportunities competes with a vanishing coherent angle per layer. Our results also reveal limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolatin strategies based on oversimplified functions.
summary: This work rigorously analyzes how fixed-depth Trotter simulation structures hardware noise by showing that the accumulated errors converge to a stationary channel. This stationarity allows for an almost time-independent correction factor at the observable level, which is crucial for developing robust error mitigation protocols in quantum computing simulations.
main_problem: The paper analyzes fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body quantum dynamics.
main_result: For large times, the noisy evolution approaches a stationary channel characterized by an almost time-independent affine contrast correction at the observable level, which is useful for error mitigation.
method: The analysis involves deriving the factorization of the noisy circuit into ideal evolution followed by a stationary binomial or Poissonian channel using superoperator techniques and moment expansions.
model_or_system: The model simulates quantum dynamics governed by local Hamiltonians (e.g., TFIM) using first-order Trotterization, subjected to local stochastic Pauli errors at each gate layer.
key_observables: Observable depolarization factor, mismatch norm $\Delta M(T)$, Loschmidt echo signal $G(t)$, and the affine contrast correction coefficients ($a_O(\mu), c_O(\mu)$).
important_parameters: Fixed depth $N$, noise dose (made endpoint-independent), mean number of faults $\mu$, and crossover time scales $T_{	ext{stat}}(\delta)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, allowing factorization into a stationary channel; approximations are made using moment expansions for large times.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the operational separation between ideal evolution and the noisy signal, showing unphysical short-time values before reaching the stationary regime.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the fixed-depth protocol, deriving the factorization into a stationary channel (binomial/Poissonian), analyzing the crossover from Zeno-like transients to stationarity, and finally comparing the mathematical rigor of the Poisson vs. binomial approximations in the large depth limit.
why_interesting: It provides concrete theoretical tools for understanding how structured noise accumulates over time in quantum simulations, offering practical insights into error mitigation techniques beyond simple depolarization models.
